newsitem.title: UK: UK's Brown says no direct levy on mobile phones.
newsitem.headline: UK's Brown says no direct levy on mobile phones.

text.p: British Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown said government plans to reform the way it charges for use of the radio spectrum did not amount to a tax on mobile phone users or taxi cabs.
"There is no direct levy on mobile phone-users," he told BBC television.
"What we're actually doing is looking at how we use the resource of the spectrum properly -- a more efficient use of the spectrum and of course a more market-pricing arrangement for dealing with it."
Asked if this meant average mobile phone-users would not face higher bills, Brown replied:
"I think the competition in the industry should be bringing prices down, but there is no direct levy on them and it is quite wrong to say that that's the case."
Brown said that by making more efficient use of the spectrum, "you would be getting charges down."
Officials said on Tuesday that the government would overhaul charging for use of the radio spectrum by broadcasters, mobile phone operators, taxi companies and other users.
The changes would generate revenue of around one billion pounds over time compared with a figure of around 40 million which is raised at present.
Brown said the proposals had been inherited from the Conservative government and were therefore bi-partisan.
"We found that only an administrative charge was being levied to cover the costs of administration for this. There should be a market pricing when this is a valuable national asset," he added.
